To oppose something means to be actively against it — not just in your mind, but through your words, stance, or actions. When you oppose something, you push back against it, resist it, or try to challenge or stop it.

Here's an important distinction: if you simply dislike something quietly and do nothing about it, that's not quite opposing. To oppose is to take a side — the side that is against something — and to clearly express or act on that position.
The Key Idea: Two Sides in Tension

Whenever "oppose" appears, there are always two sides facing each other. You, and the thing or person you are against. This tension — this push and pull — is the soul of the word. The two sides could be people, ideas, groups, or forces working against each other.
How "Oppose" Is Used in Different Situations

1. Opposing an idea, plan, or decision — this is the most common use. It means you disagree with something and actively work against it.

  • Many citizens opposed the new tax law.
  • The scientists opposed the flawed theory.
  • She opposed every change the committee proposed.

2. Opposing a person — standing against someone directly, especially in a competition, election, or conflict.

  • He will oppose the current mayor in the upcoming election.
  • The underdog was chosen to oppose the reigning champion.

3. Opposing in a debate or argument — arguing against what someone says.

  • The lawyer opposed every claim made by the other side.

4. Physical opposition — blocking or resisting something by force or position.

  • The soldiers opposed the enemy's advance into the city.
  • A locked door opposed his entry.
How Strongly Can You Oppose Something?

The word "oppose" on its own doesn't tell you how intensely someone is against something — that comes from the words used around it. Pay attention to these:

  • slightly opposed → mild disagreement
  • strongly opposed / firmly opposed → serious, clear resistance
  • bitterly opposed / vehemently opposed → deep, intense resistance, often with emotion

So "she opposed the plan" and "she bitterly opposed the plan" both use the same verb, but the second one tells you she felt very strongly about it.
The Very Common Phrase: "As Opposed To"

This phrase deserves special attention because it is used constantly in everyday English, and its meaning is slightly different from the main verb.

"As opposed to" means "in contrast to" or "rather than." It highlights a clear difference or preference between two things. Importantly, there is no conflict here — it simply draws a distinction.

  • I prefer working in the morning, as opposed to the evening.
  • This is a health issue, as opposed to a lifestyle choice.
  • She wanted a small wedding, as opposed to a large celebration.

Think of it as a way of saying: "Let's be clear — I'm talking about THIS one, not THAT one."

Learning a word fully means knowing its relatives. Here is the family of "oppose":

Opponent (noun) — a person who opposes you; your rival or adversary in a competition, debate, or conflict.
He was a skilled opponent who never gave up easily.

Opposition (noun) — this has two uses. First, it means the act of opposing something. Second, it refers to the group of people who are against something, especially in politics.
The proposal faced fierce opposition from the public.
The opposition party voted against the bill.

Opposed (adjective) — used to describe someone who is against something, or two things that are against each other.
I am completely opposed to the idea.
The two sides held opposed views on the matter.

Opposing (adjective / present participle) — describes something or someone that is on the other side.
The opposing team played brilliantly.
They came from opposing backgrounds but became close friends.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Think of the prefix "op-" as meaning "against" and the image it creates: two things facing each other from opposite sides. Whenever you see or use "oppose," picture two forces or two people standing face to face, each pushing against the other. That image captures the word perfectly.
